Design modules to be deep: maximize functionality behind the simplest interface that covers the common case.
Encapsulate each design decision inside a single module so it does not appear in any interface, and treat information leakage as a red flag.
Design interfaces so the most common usage is as simple as possible, providing sensible defaults and automatic behavior.
Make modules somewhat general-purpose: tie functionality to current needs but keep the interface general enough for multiple uses.
Organize modules around the knowledge each task needs, not the time order in which operations occur.
Give adjacent layers different abstractions; treat pass-through methods, pass-through variables, and API-duplicating decorators as red flags.
Add an interface, class, argument, or other infrastructure element only when it removes more complexity than it introduces.
Absorb unavoidable complexity inside a module rather than exposing it to users, because a simple interface matters more than a simple implementation.
Be only as generic as present known needs require; treat any design that adds complexity instead of removing it as overengineering.
Avoid configuration parameters where the system can compute a good value itself, and compute sensible defaults automatically.
Combine code that is closely related (shared information, used together, conceptual overlap) and separate only components that are truly independent.
Keep every piece of information and logic in exactly one place, and reuse code instead of copying and pasting.
Keep general-purpose mechanisms free of special-purpose code, pushing special-purpose code into higher layers.
Decide whether to split or join a method by whether it yields cleaner abstractions, not by line count; each method should do one thing completely.
Reduce the number of places exceptions must be handled, ideally by redefining operation semantics so the normal case has no error to report.
Mask a low-level exception so higher levels need not handle it, where the exception information is not needed above the handling layer.
Aggregate many exceptions into a single high-level handler positioned where it catches the most exceptions.
For rare errors with no useful recovery, abort with a clear diagnostic instead of adding handling complexity.
Eliminate special cases by designing the normal case to handle them automatically; hide the unimportant and expose the important.
Consider multiple genuinely different designs for each major decision before choosing one.
Write interface comments before code so documentation drives the design, and read long comments as a canary for poor abstractions.
Write comments to capture what is not obvious from the code, and never write comments that merely repeat the code.
Use lower-level comments for precision and higher-level comments for intuition, and separate interface comments from implementation comments.
Choose names that are precise, intuitive, and used consistently; treat a hard-to-name entity as a design red flag.
Keep documentation close to and inside the code (not the commit log), and document each design decision exactly once.
When modifying existing code, leave the design at least slightly better - ideally as if it had been designed with the change in mind from the start.

Optimize for changeability: the real test of good code is how easily it can be changed, so favor clarity over brevity, write code primarily for the future human reader, and always leave the codebase healthier than you found it.
Make similar things work similarly: follow existing conventions, document and enforce them, and do not change a convention just because you have a better idea.
Write obvious code (good names, consistency, white space, conforming to expectations); judge obviousness by readers and design for reading rather than writing.
Judge simplicity from the target audience's viewpoint, which for code is other programmers, and write for someone who knows nothing about the system.
Make code easy to read using consistent, structure-revealing spacing and good names, since code is read more than written and readable code is easier to fix.
Develop in increments of abstractions, not features; once an abstraction is needed, design it cleanly and somewhat general-purpose all at once.
Make design decisions from present, known information and keep code flexible for change, without trying to predict specific future requirements.
Use OO mechanisms, inheritance, and design patterns only where they reduce complexity; prefer composition over implementation inheritance and avoid exposing instance variables.

Hide implementation behind abstractions: keep variables private, expose interfaces that manipulate the essence of the data, and do not blindly add getters and setters, because exposing variables through accessors still exposes implementation.
Favour object composition over class inheritance for reuse, because composition is black-box, keeps encapsulation intact, and can be reconfigured at run time.
Maintain a good unit-test suite so refactoring is safe and the design can keep improving.
Maintain an automated suite of covering unit tests, because tests are what keep a design flexible, maintainable, and reusable by removing the fear that blocks change and refactoring.

Write clean code by successive refinement under a covering test suite: first make it work, then make it right, refactoring in many tiny verified steps and stopping to fix the structure before a mess grows too large, never via a big-bang rewrite.

Keep refactoring behavior-preserving and separate from other work: wear one hat at a time (refactor vs add functionality), change only internal structure, and treat refactoring as distinct from performance optimization, whose goals differ.

Treat a fast, self-checking, self-testing suite as a prerequisite for refactoring: automate the tests, make them check their own results, run them frequently, and confirm each test can fail when it should.

Refactor when change demands it: refactor first to make a feature or bug fix easy (preparatory), refactor to understand unfamiliar code (comprehension), remove duplication by the rule of three, and fold refactoring opportunistically into everyday work because software is never done.

Do not over- or mis-apply refactoring: leave messy code you do not need to touch, keep dedicated planned-refactoring episodes rare, occasionally rewrite instead of refactor, and justify refactoring on economic grounds (faster delivery) rather than moral or aesthetic ones.
Refactor legacy code safely by first getting it under test through seams, then improving it in small pieces as you pass through, doing the most work in the areas you visit most.
Achieve performance through simplicity: choose naturally efficient clean designs, measure before optimizing, and design around the critical path.
Define the software's purpose as helping people and use 'how much does this help?' as the primary test for every design decision and feature priority.
Optimize design to minimize long-term maintenance effort rather than implementation effort, since over a system's lifetime maintenance dominates the desirability of changes.
Prefer designs whose maintenance effort decreases over time toward zero, and reject changes whose maintenance grows faster than their value.
Keep changes small to lower defect risk, enable real design on each change, and reduce maintenance effort.
Scale design effort to how long the system will keep helping people; when in doubt, assume a long life and invest in design accordingly.
Invest in design continuously, because systems do not become simple on their own and an undesigned growing system drifts into failing complexity.
Do not write code until it is actually needed, and delete code that isn't being used.
Write comments that explain why, not what; if what the code does isn't obvious, simplify the code instead of commenting it.
Build and redesign the system piece by piece, simplest part first, redesigning to make the next feature easy before implementing it.
Make each individual piece of the system as simple as possible and keep it that way, since ease of maintenance is proportional to the simplicity of the pieces.
Never fix or optimize without evidence that a real problem exists; treat a behavior as a bug only when a significant number of users do, and optimize only proven hot spots.
Aim for extreme, stupid-dumb simplicity; it broadens your users and reduces the support burden, and advanced technology is fine when it serves that simplicity.
Do things the same way everywhere and make the program behave consistently internally; when full simplicity is impossible, at least be consistent.
Keep the system's basic purpose narrow and protect it; do not expand the purpose or let misaligned stakeholders add unrelated features.
Evaluate any technology for survival potential, interoperability, and attention to quality, preferring broadly adopted, standard-based options to avoid lock-in.
Do not build large in-house infrastructure such as a web server, protocol, or major library unless it is your product or every existing option is unusable.
When complexity appears, look for the underlying design error, redesign pieces in small steps without adding complexity, and hide truly unfixable complexity behind a simple wrapper.
Prefer incremental redesign to rewriting; rewrite only when all of the rare conditions hold, and never stop maintaining a system in use to rewrite it.
Know your software only to the degree you have accurately tested it; you do not know it works unless you have tried it, so retest after every change, ideally with automated tests.

Name variables, functions, and classes with intention-revealing, unambiguous, pronounceable, searchable names that say why they exist, what they do, and how they are used; if a name needs a comment to be understood, it has failed.
Keep a consistent, non-cute vocabulary: one word per concept, no puns, names drawn from the solution or problem domain, and a name that reveals every effect of a function including its side effects.

Avoid name encodings (Hungarian notation, member or interface prefixes) and gratuitous context, size a name to its scope, name classes as nouns and methods as verbs, and rename freely with tools when a better name appears.
Name variables, fields, and functions to reveal intent, and rename them freely as understanding improves; difficulty finding a good name often signals a deeper design problem.

Keep functions small and doing exactly one thing, with all statements at one level of abstraction one step below the function name, blocks reduced to a call, indentation shallow, and code ordered top-down by the stepdown rule.

Prefer small, well-named functions that separate intention from implementation: extract a fragment into a function named after what it does whenever you would otherwise write a comment, and inline functions whose indirection no longer earns its keep.
Move code to better boundaries as understanding grows: relocate statements into or out of functions, slide related statements together, and substitute a whole algorithm when a clearer one is found.

Minimize function arguments (zero, then one, then two; avoid three or more), forbid flag/boolean arguments by splitting the function, avoid output arguments by mutating the owning object, and wrap groups of related arguments in a class.

A function must have no hidden side effects and obey Command-Query Separation - it either changes state or returns information, never both; if a temporal coupling is unavoidable, make it explicit in the name and argument structure.

Use descriptive function names and prefer polymorphism to switch/if-else chains; tolerate a switch only when it appears once, creates polymorphic objects, and is hidden behind an inheritance relationship.

Simplify conditional logic: decompose complex conditions into intention-named functions, use guard clauses for unusual cases, and replace type-code switching with polymorphism — but reserve polymorphism for type-based or base-plus-variant cases rather than converting all conditionals.

Prefer throwing exceptions to returning error codes, write the try-catch-finally scope first, give every exception enough context to locate and log it, classify exceptions by how they are caught, and prefer unchecked exceptions in general application code.
Do not return or pass null; return an empty collection, throw, or use the Special Case pattern, and forbid null arguments by default so a null signals a real problem.

Treat comments as a last resort and a necessary evil; first try to express the intent in code, since the code is the only reliable source of truth and comments decay into lies as they drift from the code they describe.

Keep surviving comments truthful, brief, and local: delete redundant, mandated, noise, obsolete, journal, and authorship comments and all commented-out code, and let source control hold history; reserve comments for technical notes the code cannot express.

Apply one agreed team formatting style enforced by a tool, keep source files small, and structure each file newspaper-style with high-level concepts first, vertical openness between concepts, vertical closeness of related code, and short lines.

Choose objects (hide data, expose behavior) versus data structures (expose data, no behavior) by which axis the system will grow - new types favor objects, new functions favor procedural data structures - and never build hybrids that are half of each.

Obey the Law of Demeter: a method should call methods only on its own class, objects it creates, its arguments, and its instance variables, talking to friends not strangers, and avoid train-wreck and transitive navigation chains.

Isolate every third-party or not-yet-built boundary behind a wrapper or Adapter you control, referenced in few places and supported by learning tests and boundary tests, so the external API can change with minimal impact.

Drive production code with the Three Laws of TDD - no production code without a failing test, no more test than fails, no more production code than passes - writing each unit test just before the code that makes it pass.

Keep test code as clean as production code: readable above all, one concept per test with minimal asserts, built-operate-check structure, a domain-specific testing language, and F.I.R.S.T. (fast, independent, repeatable, self-validating, timely).

Test everything that could break: use a coverage tool to find gaps, write a test for every boundary and corner case, test trivial cases, exhaustively test near a found bug, and read patterns of failure and coverage as diagnostic clues.

Make testing risk-driven and bug-finding: concentrate tests on complex code and boundary conditions, start a bug fix by writing a failing test that exposes it, and judge a suite by confidence that a defect would trip a test rather than by coverage percentage.

Keep classes small and single-responsibility (exactly one reason to change), measured by counting responsibilities; prefer many small, highly cohesive classes over a few large ones, and split a class when its cohesion drops.

Manage inheritance deliberately: pull common members up and push specific members down, remove subclasses that no longer earn their keep, and replace subclassing with delegation when you need more than one axis of variation or the subclass is not a true subtype — favoring composition over inheritance.

Structure classes to be open for extension but closed for modification and to depend on abstractions rather than concrete details (inject dependencies), acting on this when real change forces you to open a class rather than speculatively.

Separate constructing a system from using it: move object construction and dependency wiring into main, factories, or a dependency-injection container so application objects stay passive and unaware of how they were built.
Use a creational pattern to decouple a system from how its objects are created, composed, and represented.

Grow architecture incrementally instead of Big Design Up Front, keeping domain logic in framework-free POJOs with cross-cutting concerns applied noninvasively, and always use the simplest thing that can possibly work.
Defer decisions to the last responsible moment so they are made with the most knowledge, and adopt standards or domain-specific languages only when they add demonstrable value.

Follow the four rules of Simple Design in priority order - the design runs all the tests, contains no duplication, expresses the programmer's intent, and minimizes the number of classes and methods - treating entity-count reduction as the lowest priority.

Eliminate duplication relentlessly, since every duplication is a missed abstraction: fold identical code into a method, repeated conditionals into polymorphism, and similar algorithms into a Template Method or Strategy.
Eliminate duplicated knowledge so the system says everything once and only once, unifying repeated code with extraction, parameterization, or a shared function call.

Treat concurrency as a hard, separate concern with its own reason to change: keep concurrency code apart from other code, and reject the myths that it always improves performance, leaves design unchanged, or is handled for you by a container.

Manage locking deliberately: know the concurrency library and execution models, beware dependencies between synchronized methods, and prefer server-based locking over client-based locking (wrapping with an Adapter when you do not own the server).

Minimize and isolate shared mutable data: severely limit its scope, prefer copies and read-only objects, make threads as independent as possible working from local data, and keep synchronized sections as small as possible.

Prevent deadlock by understanding its four necessary conditions (mutual exclusion, lock-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) and deliberately breaking one - most commonly by imposing a global resource-acquisition order to break circular wait.

Test threaded code aggressively: get nonthreaded logic working first in thread-ignorant POJOs, make the thread-aware code pluggable and tunable, run with more threads than processors and on every target platform, and instrument it to force orderings - never write a failure off as a one-off.

It is not enough for code to work; keep it clean continuously and leave every module cleaner than you found it (the Boy Scout Rule), because deferred cleanup never happens and bad code rots into a weight that drags the team down.

The only way to go fast is to keep the code clean at all times; as a professional, defend code quality against schedule pressure, and remember these rules express a value system rather than a rote checklist.

Optimize for readability, since code is read far more than it is written: make intent visible with good names, small functions, explanatory variables, and conditionals encapsulated in intent-revealing positive predicates.

Apply least-surprise structural heuristics: implement the behavior a reader would reasonably expect, keep concepts at the right level of abstraction with base classes independent of derivatives, put each responsibility where it is expected, and never override safeties.

Make dependencies and constants explicit: replace magic numbers and tokens with named constants, encapsulate boundary arithmetic in one named place, make logical dependencies physical by asking rather than assuming, and keep configurable data at high levels passed downward.

Be precise and prefer structure to convention: handle nulls, currency, locking, and type constraints deliberately, prefer nonstatic to static, keep interfaces minimal, avoid artificial coupling, and delete dead code and clutter.
Understand your algorithm well enough to know it is correct rather than just passing tests, and keep a method interested in its own class's data rather than envying another's.

Refactor in tiny behavior-preserving steps, compiling and running the tests after each step and committing after each success; when a step breaks the tests and the cause is not obvious, revert to the last green commit and redo with smaller steps.

Keep tests isolated and readable: build a fresh fixture before each test rather than sharing mutable state, prefer a single assertion per test, and separate business logic from UI, persistence, and external services so it can be tested in isolation.

Favor continuous integration over long-lived feature branches, prefer team ownership over fine-grained code ownership, and when changing a published interface keep the old declaration as a deprecated pass-through until clients migrate.

Pursue performance by writing well-factored, tunable code first and optimizing last: measure with a profiler instead of speculating, target the small fraction of hot-spot code, and tune in small measured steps, backing out changes that do not help.

Practice evolutionary design (YAGNI): build software that excellently solves only the currently understood needs and adapt it by refactoring, adding a flexibility mechanism now only when refactoring it in later would be substantially harder.

Minimize and encapsulate mutable and global data: route access through functions, restrict scope, prefer immutability, remove setters for fields that should not change, and replace derived variables with queries.

Co-locate behavior with the data it uses and cut inappropriate coupling between modules: move a function or field to the data it most references, and reduce excessive chatting between modules (feature envy, message chains, middle man, insider trading) with moves, delegation hiding, or a shared module.

Keep parameter lists short and meaningful: combine data clumps into a parameter object, pass a whole record instead of several of its fields, replace a flag argument with explicit functions, and drop a parameter the function could compute itself.
Form classes or transforms around a common body of data, split classes that have grown too big, and create first-class domain types for primitives that have gained behavior.
Clarify expressions and temporaries: introduce explaining variables for complex sub-expressions, replace a write-once temporary with a query, and inline a variable whose name adds nothing.

Separate distinct responsibilities structurally: split sequential concerns into phases with a clear intermediate data structure, split a loop that does two things, and split a variable that carries more than one responsibility.
Remove what no longer pays its way: replace loops with collection pipelines, delete dead code rather than commenting it out, strip speculative generality, and inline lazy elements that add no value.

Encapsulate records, collections, and construction: hide collection internals behind add/remove methods, prefer factory functions over constructors when you need flexibility, and use a command object only when a plain function cannot provide a needed facility.
Program to an interface, not an implementation: have client code depend on abstract types, not concrete classes, so implementations can change without breaking clients.
Use Adapter to make a class with an incompatible interface usable by converting its interface to the one clients expect.
Encapsulate what varies: isolate the design aspect that changes behind a stable interface so that change to it does not ripple through the system.

Treat patterns as a shared vocabulary and as targets for refactoring; classify a recurring problem by purpose (creational/structural/behavioral) and scope (class/object) to narrow the candidate patterns.
Use Abstract Factory to create families of related products through one interface; expect easy swapping of whole families but costly addition of a new product kind.
Use Factory Method to let subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate when a class cannot anticipate the class of objects it must create.
Use Prototype to create new objects by cloning a prototypical instance, e.g. when the classes to instantiate are specified at run time or to avoid a parallel factory hierarchy.
Use Builder to separate the construction of a complex object from its representation so one construction process can yield different representations.
Use Singleton only when exactly one instance of a class must exist with a single global access point.
Use Bridge to decouple an abstraction from its implementation so both hierarchies can be extended and vary independently.
Use Composite to model part-whole hierarchies and let clients treat leaves and composites uniformly, while watching for over-generality.
Use Decorator to add or remove responsibilities to an object dynamically as a flexible alternative to subclassing, keeping the component's interface unchanged.
Use Facade to give a complex subsystem a single, higher-level interface that makes it simpler to use and decouples it from its clients.
Use Flyweight to share many fine-grained objects efficiently by splitting their state into shared intrinsic state and supplied extrinsic state.
Use Proxy to provide a surrogate that controls access to another object, e.g. to defer cost, restrict access, or add location transparency.
Prefer Strategy over conditional statements to select among interchangeable algorithms, letting the algorithm vary independently of the clients that use it.
Use the State pattern (a separate object per state) to make state-dependent behaviour and its transitions explicit rather than implicit in conditionals.
Use Observer to keep dependents consistent with a subject through a one-to-many dependency while keeping them loosely coupled.
Use Template Method to fix an algorithm's skeleton in a base operation and defer the varying steps to subclass hook operations.
Use Visitor to add new operations over a stable object structure without changing the element classes, accepting that adding new element types becomes costly.
Use Command to encapsulate a request as an object so requests can be parameterized, queued, logged, and undone.
Use Mediator to centralize complex many-to-many interaction and decouple colleagues, accepting the risk that the mediator itself becomes a hard-to-maintain monolith.
Use Memento to capture and restore an object's state without violating encapsulation; the caretaker stores the memento but must not inspect its contents.
Use Iterator to traverse an aggregate sequentially without exposing its representation, choosing external versus internal control deliberately.
Use Chain of Responsibility to decouple a request's sender from its receiver by letting multiple handlers each get a chance to handle it in sequence.
Use Interpreter to represent a simple, stable grammar as a class hierarchy and interpret its sentences.
